executive_summary: Cricket S&C planning should be role-led, phase-led, and workload-aware. The same athlete may accumulate sprinting, repeated accelerations, rotational hitting, bowling, throwing, crouching, diving, and long-duration field exposure in one week, so the backend should treat cricket as a combined skill-load and physical-load system rather than a generic gym plan. Fast bowlers need the strongest workload guardrails because lumbar bone stress injury risk is shaped by age, maturation, bowling volume, recent spikes, technique, trunk mechanics, and prior back symptoms. All players need a fielding and throwing durability layer; batters need repeat sprint and rotational power support; spinners need shoulder, trunk, forearm, wrist, and finger capacity; wicketkeepers need hip, ankle, adductor, quad, trunk, hand, and reaction capacity; all-rounders need conflict management because their total cricket load can exceed the load of specialist roles. Off-season should rebuild strength, tissue capacity, sprint mechanics, mobility, and broad athletic qualities while skill volume is lower. Pre-season should progressively reintroduce bowling, throwing, sprinting, and match-simulation density. In-season should maintain strength and power, preserve high-speed exposure, monitor bowling and throwing load, and trim gym stress around heavy match or bowling weeks. Return-to-bowling should be staged, symptom-led, and clinician-supervised after lumbar, shoulder, side strain, hamstring, adductor, wrist, or finger injury. Useful testing should combine objective outputs, movement capacity, role-specific skill load, and athlete-state trends instead of relying on single population benchmarks.

key_concepts.title: Role-first planning
key_concepts.summary: Cricket training should begin with the athlete's primary and secondary roles: batter, fast bowler, spinner, all-rounder, wicketkeeper, fielder, or role combinations. Role determines the dominant stressors, injury risks, match-week conflicts, and testing priorities.
key_concepts.backend_use: Use role tags before selecting sport demands, risk rules, and session emphasis.
sources: Cricket Research Master Plan
Injuries in Cricket
Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Fielding

key_concepts.title: Skill load is training load
key_concepts.summary: Cricket practice can include high mechanical stress even when it does not look like conditioning. Bowling balls, throwing repetitions, sprinting between wickets, diving, and long fielding stints should all update athlete state.
key_concepts.backend_use: Track skill exposure alongside gym sessions, running, and readiness.
sources: Bowling Workload and the Risk of Injury in Elite Cricket Fast Bowlers
Relationship Between Cricket Workload and Injury Risk

key_concepts.title: Bowling load spikes matter
key_concepts.summary: Fast bowling injury risk is associated with recent changes in workload as well as accumulated workload. Acute spikes after low bowling exposure are especially relevant after holidays, injury breaks, exams, or rain-disrupted seasons.
key_concepts.backend_use: Flag rapid increases in balls or overs and avoid stacking intense gym stress in the same week.
sources: Spikes in Acute Workload Are Associated With Increased Injury Risk in Elite Cricket Fast Bowlers
Is Bowling Workload a Risk Factor for Injury to Australian Junior Cricket Fast Bowlers

key_concepts.title: Youth progression is maturation-sensitive
key_concepts.summary: Young pace bowlers have additional risk because high bowling load may coincide with growth, incomplete skeletal maturity, technique changes, and uneven strength development. Progression should be conservative and broad-athletic before specialized.
key_concepts.backend_use: Use age and maturation flags to constrain fast bowling volume, intensity, and gym progression.
sources: Cricket Australia Junior Pace Bowling Workload Guidelines
Injury Prevention Strategies for Adolescent Cricket Pace Bowlers
NSCA Position Statement on Long-Term Athletic Development

key_concepts.title: Throwing is separate from bowling
key_concepts.summary: Throwing uses a different pattern from bowling and can accumulate high shoulder, elbow, trunk, and hip stress during warm-ups, fielding drills, wicketkeeping returns, and boundary fielding. A bowler can be under-recovered from throwing even if bowling volume is controlled.
key_concepts.backend_use: Track throwing volume, intensity, distance, and symptoms independently from bowling.
sources: Shoulder Injuries in Modern Cricket
ASCA Review of Throwing Speed Determinants
Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Fielding

key_concepts.title: Every role needs a fielding layer
key_concepts.summary: Even specialist batters and bowlers must accelerate, decelerate, dive, catch, throw, and maintain concentration for long periods. Fielding should not be treated as optional accessory work.
key_concepts.backend_use: Add universal sprint, deceleration, trunk, shoulder, hand, and landing demands to all cricket roles.
sources: Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Fielding
Injuries in Cricket

key_concepts.title: Season phase changes the goal
key_concepts.summary: Off-season can build physical qualities aggressively because match and skill load are lower. Pre-season should bridge physical work into cricket-specific speed, bowling, throwing, and match density. In-season should maintain outputs, manage fatigue, and prevent workload spikes.
key_concepts.backend_use: Map macro plan blocks to off-season, pre-season, in-season, finals/tournament, and return-to-play states.
sources: NSCA Injury Prevention Strategies in Cricket
Workout AI Backend Plan

key_concepts.title: Benchmarks need individual baselines
key_concepts.summary: Cricket testing should use population benchmarks cautiously. Sprint times, jump scores, Yo-Yo performance, strength numbers, shoulder range, trunk endurance, and bowling outputs are most useful when compared to the athlete's own role, level, age, sex, and recent trend.
key_concepts.backend_use: Store absolute results and rolling changes, not only pass/fail thresholds.
sources: Physical Profiling of International Cricket Players
Anthropometry and Physical Profile of Elite Female Cricket Fast Bowlers

key_concepts.title: Pain is a planning input
key_concepts.summary: Back pain in a fast bowler, throwing shoulder pain, side pain with bowling, groin pain during acceleration, and finger or wrist pain in spinners should alter the training plan before the next heavy exposure.
key_concepts.backend_use: Treat pain location and trend as higher-priority constraints than planned progression.
sources: Management of Lumbar Spine-Related Stress Injuries in Cricket Fast Bowlers
Injuries in Cricket

key_concepts.title: All-rounders need conflict management
key_concepts.summary: All-rounders may combine specialist bowling load, batting sprint load, fielding load, and gym load. Their key risk is not one quality missing, but too many moderate-to-high exposures stacked without recovery.
key_concepts.backend_use: Calculate weekly total load across bowling, batting, throwing, sprinting, match minutes, and gym stress.
sources: Relationship Between Cricket Workload and Injury Risk
Injuries in Cricket

technical_models.title: Role-phase-load model
technical_models.model: cricket_plan = role + match_format + season_phase + skill_load + gym_load + injury_flags + readiness + facilities
technical_models.details: The backend should not retrieve the same S&C rules for a fast bowler in pre-season, a wicketkeeper during a tournament week, and a recreational batter returning from hamstring pain.
sources: Workout AI Backend Plan
Cricket Research Master Plan

technical_models.title: Season macrocycle model
technical_models.model: off-season -> pre-season -> early in-season -> competition maintenance -> tournament/finals compression -> transition
technical_models.details: Off-season emphasizes strength, mobility, aerobic base, sprint mechanics, and tissue capacity. Pre-season progressively adds cricket-specific bowling, throwing, sprinting, and match simulation. In-season reduces total gym volume but keeps strength, power, mobility, and injury-prevention doses.
sources: NSCA Injury Prevention Strategies in Cricket
NSCA Position Statement on Long-Term Athletic Development

technical_models.title: One-match-week microcycle model
technical_models.model: match_day + 1 recovery; match_day + 2 moderate strength or capacity; match_day - 3 main strength/power if recovered; match_day - 2 skill speed rehearsal; match_day - 1 primer; match_day compete
technical_models.details: For Saturday matches, heavy lower-body strength is usually best placed early to midweek, not the day before play. Fast bowlers with high midweek bowling should have lower gym volume and avoid heavy spinal loading near bowling spikes.
sources: NSCA Injury Prevention Strategies in Cricket
ECB Recreational Fast Bowling Guidance 2024

technical_models.title: Fast bowling workload model
technical_models.model: track balls or overs by session, week, spell, intensity, rest days, last 7 days, last 28 days, and change from prior exposure
technical_models.details: Official youth and recreational guidance sets maximum balls, overs, spells, and rest principles. Peer-reviewed studies support monitoring both recent spikes and medium-term accumulated workload.
sources: Cricket Australia Junior Pace Bowling Workload Guidelines
ECB Recreational Fast Bowling Guidance 2024
Spikes in Acute Workload Are Associated With Increased Injury Risk in Elite Cricket Fast Bowlers

technical_models.title: Fast bowler lumbar bone stress risk model
technical_models.model: risk = maturation + prior back pain + bowling workload + workload spike + technique + trunk strength/endurance + hip mobility + recovery
technical_models.details: Lumbar bone stress injury risk is multi-factorial. Technique features such as excessive shoulder counter-rotation or mixed bowling action are commonly discussed, but load, symptoms, maturity, and imaging/clinical assessment remain central.
sources: Management of Lumbar Spine-Related Stress Injuries in Cricket Fast Bowlers
MRI Findings and Lumbar Bone Stress Injury in Fast Bowlers
Fast Bowling Kinematics and Lumbar Spine Injuries

technical_models.title: Throwing kinetic-chain model
technical_models.model: throwing output = lower-body force + trunk rotation + scapular control + shoulder rotation strength + elbow/wrist transfer + technique + recovery
technical_models.details: Throwing speed is not a shoulder-only output. S&C should build whole-body power and shoulder durability while fielding coaches manage technique and progressive throw distance/intensity.
sources: ASCA Review of Throwing Speed Determinants
Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Fielding
Shoulder Injuries in Modern Cricket

technical_models.title: Return-to-bowling model
technical_models.model: pain-free daily function -> clinical clearance -> low-intensity technical bowling -> controlled volume -> controlled intensity -> spell simulation -> match simulation -> competition
technical_models.details: Return-to-bowling should be staged and symptom-led, with volume and intensity not progressed together. Back stress, side strain, shoulder pain, and lower-limb injuries each need different progression speeds.
sources: Management of Lumbar Spine-Related Stress Injuries in Cricket Fast Bowlers
ECB Recreational Fast Bowling Guidance 2024

technical_models.title: Cricket athlete-state dashboard
technical_models.model: readiness + sleep + soreness + pain map + balls bowled + throws + sprints + gym RPE + match exposure + testing trend
technical_models.details: Monitoring should combine external load, internal response, and symptoms. A low-readiness athlete with rising back soreness and a bowling spike should receive different training than a well-recovered athlete with stable exposure.
sources: Is Bowling Workload a Risk Factor for Injury to Australian Junior Cricket Fast Bowlers
Relationship Between Cricket Workload and Injury Risk
Workout AI Backend Plan

tactical_rules.rule: New or worsening lumbar pain in a fast bowler should stop high-intensity bowling and heavy spinal loading until assessed by an appropriate clinician.
training_response: replace bowling with pain-free mobility, low-load trunk work, and non-provocative conditioning
do not progress bowling volume while symptoms rise
sources: Management of Lumbar Spine-Related Stress Injuries in Cricket Fast Bowlers
Injury Prevention Strategies for Adolescent Cricket Pace Bowlers

tactical_rules.rule: Cricket Australia's youth guidance uses the 1-3-5 and 2-4-6 principles: under-13 bowlers should bowl at least 1 over per bowling day and no more than 3 days per week with no more than 5 overs per day; under-14 to under-19 bowlers should bowl at least 2 overs per bowling day and no more than 4 days per week with no more than 6 overs per day.
training_response: use these as hard caps unless a qualified governing-body or medical plan is more conservative
avoid adding intense lower-back gym stress on heavy bowling days
sources: Cricket Australia Junior Pace Bowling Workload Guidelines

tactical_rules.rule: ECB recreational guidance emphasizes age-band bowling limits, spell management, rest, and gradual build-up rather than large isolated spells. The app should retrieve the exact age-band limit rather than infer one from adult norms.
training_response: cap session bowling by age and format
insert non-bowling days or lower-intensity technical days when match and training overs are high
sources: ECB Recreational Fast Bowling Guidance 2024

tactical_rules.rule: If bowling load rises sharply from the athlete's recent baseline, reduce lower-body eccentric volume, heavy axial loading, lateral flexion fatigue, maximal sprint density, and extra bowling volume for the same week.
training_response: swap maximal strength for maintenance strength or mobility
keep high-quality movement but reduce total mechanical stress
sources: Spikes in Acute Workload Are Associated With Increased Injury Risk in Elite Cricket Fast Bowlers
Relationship Between Cricket Workload and Injury Risk

tactical_rules.rule: Within 24 to 36 hours of a match, avoid new exercises, high-volume eccentric lower-body work, heavy trunk fatigue, and exhaustive conditioning unless the athlete is in a planned conditioning block with no performance priority.
training_response: use short primers, mobility, low-volume power, catching, and technical rhythm
prioritize sleep, hydration, and symptom checks
sources: NSCA Injury Prevention Strategies in Cricket

tactical_rules.rule: Progress throw distance, intensity, and count separately; do not increase all three in the same week, especially after shoulder, elbow, side, or trunk symptoms.
training_response: count high-intensity boundary throws and wicketkeeper returns
include shoulder external rotation, scapular, trunk, and deceleration capacity work
sources: Shoulder Injuries in Modern Cricket
ASCA Review of Throwing Speed Determinants

tactical_rules.rule: For spinners, manage wrist, finger, forearm, and shoulder symptoms as skill-load constraints, not minor discomfort. High-repetition variation practice can overload small joints even when whole-body fatigue seems low.
training_response: alternate high-spin repetition days with lower-volume control days
add progressive forearm, grip, wrist, finger, shoulder, and trunk capacity work
sources: Injuries in Cricket
NSCA Injury Prevention Strategies in Cricket

tactical_rules.rule: After long wicketkeeping exposure, reduce next-day squat volume, deep knee-flexion isometrics, plyometric density, and high-volume adductor work if hip, knee, back, or groin soreness is elevated.
training_response: prioritize hip and ankle mobility, tissue recovery, trunk endurance, and low-load movement quality before heavy lower-body work
sources: Wicket-Keeping in Cricket: A Literature Review
Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Wicket-Keeping

tactical_rules.rule: When an all-rounder completes meaningful batting, bowling, and fielding load in the same day, the next training dose should be decided from total cricket stress rather than by only the planned gym calendar.
training_response: downgrade next-day intensity if soreness, readiness, or pain trends are poor
maintain mobility and low-volume strength if recovery is good
sources: Relationship Between Cricket Workload and Injury Risk
Injuries in Cricket

physical_demands.summary: Batters need acceleration between wickets, repeat sprint ability, braking and turning mechanics, rotational power, trunk stiffness, bat-speed support, hamstring and calf capacity, and the ability to repeat skill under fatigue.
sources: Physical Demands of Batting and Fast Bowling in Cricket
Physical Profiling of International Cricket Players

physical_demands.summary: Short-format finishers need higher emphasis on rotational power, upper-body contribution, fast acceleration from low starts, aggressive turning, and maintaining decision quality under high arousal.
sources: Physical Demands of Batting and Fast Bowling in Cricket

physical_demands.summary: Fast bowlers need run-up speed, repeat sprint tolerance, lower-body force, front-leg bracing tolerance, hip-shoulder separation control, trunk stiffness, trunk endurance, shoulder capacity, and aerobic support between spells.
sources: Physical Demands of Batting and Fast Bowling in Cricket
Fast Bowling Kinematics and Lumbar Spine Injuries

physical_demands.summary: Youth fast bowlers need technical consistency, gradual bowling exposure, general strength, landing and sprint mechanics, mobility, trunk endurance, and growth-aware load control before aggressive specialization.
sources: Cricket Australia Junior Pace Bowling Workload Guidelines
Injury Prevention Strategies for Adolescent Cricket Pace Bowlers

physical_demands.summary: Spinners need repeatable rhythm, shoulder durability, trunk rotation and anti-rotation strength, hip mobility, forearm endurance, wrist and finger capacity, and the ability to maintain release quality over long spells.
sources: Injuries in Cricket
NSCA Injury Prevention Strategies in Cricket

physical_demands.summary: All-rounders combine bowling, batting, and fielding demands, so they need high durability, aerobic support, power, sprint ability, throwing capacity, and weekly load management across multiple stress types.
sources: Injuries in Cricket
Relationship Between Cricket Workload and Injury Risk

physical_demands.summary: Wicketkeepers need hip and ankle mobility, repeated squat tolerance, quad and adductor endurance, lateral movement, trunk endurance, reaction speed, hand and forearm capacity, and throwing durability.
sources: Wicket-Keeping in Cricket: A Literature Review
Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Wicket-Keeping

physical_demands.summary: All fielders need acceleration, deceleration, change of direction, repeated sprint ability, catching skill under movement, landing control, diving tolerance, shoulder and elbow durability, and trunk rotation capacity.
sources: Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Fielding

physical_demands.summary: Close fielders need fast reaction, low stance tolerance, lateral first-step speed, hand speed, concentration, and resilience to impact or awkward catches.
sources: Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Fielding

physical_demands.summary: Outfielders need longer sprint capacity, curved running, braking near the boundary, diving or sliding tolerance, long throwing power, relay throwing, and repeated high-intensity efforts with long low-intensity gaps.
sources: Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Fielding
ASCA Review of Throwing Speed Determinants

physical_demands.summary: Adult recreational players often have irregular exposure, work/life fatigue, and sudden weekend match spikes. Their plans should prioritize tissue capacity, gradual exposure, warm-up quality, and recovery consistency.
sources: ECB Recreational Fast Bowling Guidance 2024
Injuries in Cricket

physical_demands.summary: Tournament cricket compresses matches, travel, warm-ups, and recovery. The priority shifts from physical development to load triage, hydration, tissue maintenance, warm-up consistency, and availability.
sources: Injuries in Cricket
Workout AI Backend Plan

injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Fast bowling exposes the lumbar spine to repeated extension, rotation, and side-flexion forces. Young and high-volume bowlers are especially important to monitor.
sources: Management of Lumbar Spine-Related Stress Injuries in Cricket Fast Bowlers
MRI Findings and Lumbar Bone Stress Injury in Fast Bowlers

injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Biomechanical factors such as excessive counter-rotation, lateral trunk flexion, front-leg bracing demands, and inconsistent action may increase tissue stress when volume or intensity is high.
sources: Fast Bowling Kinematics and Lumbar Spine Injuries
Management of Lumbar Spine-Related Stress Injuries in Cricket Fast Bowlers

injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Some research reports injury associations after recent workload spikes and after medium-term high bowling loads. The backend should look beyond the current session and inspect multiweek trends.
sources: Spikes in Acute Workload Are Associated With Increased Injury Risk in Elite Cricket Fast Bowlers
Is Bowling Workload a Risk Factor for Injury to Australian Junior Cricket Fast Bowlers

injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Too little recent bowling exposure can leave bowlers underprepared for match spells. Sudden match exposure after low practice volume is a different risk from gradual high fitness.
planning_flags: low recent balls then match selection
sources: Relationship Between Cricket Workload and Injury Risk
ECB Recreational Fast Bowling Guidance 2024

injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: High-intensity throws, long throws, and repeated warm-up throws can overload shoulder and elbow structures, especially when scapular control, rotation strength, or trunk contribution is poor.
sources: Shoulder Injuries in Modern Cricket
ASCA Review of Throwing Speed Determinants

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Side strain and abdominal oblique injury
injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Bowling and throwing require high trunk rotation and side-flexion forces. Side strains can be aggravated by bowling intensity, throwing, and heavy rotational training too soon.
sources: Injuries in Cricket
Imaging in Elite and Recreational Cricket Injuries

injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Cricket includes repeated accelerations, sharp turns, run-ups, and fielding sprints. Hamstring risk rises when sprint exposure is absent and then suddenly reintroduced.
sources: Injuries in Cricket
Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Fielding

injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Lateral movement, wide batting stances, wicketkeeping crouches, diving, sprint turns, and bowling delivery positions can stress the adductors and groin.
sources: Injuries in Cricket
Wicket-Keeping in Cricket: A Literature Review

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Knee, ankle, calf, and Achilles overload
injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Run-ups, repeated starts, stopping, diving, uneven grounds, and long spells of standing can create lower-limb overload, especially when running and plyometric exposure are irregular.
sources: Injuries in Cricket
Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Fielding

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Spinner wrist, finger, and forearm overload
injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Finger spin and wrist spin place repeated stress through small joints and forearm tissues. Variation practice and wet-ball gripping can increase local load.
sources: Injuries in Cricket
NSCA Injury Prevention Strategies in Cricket

injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Repeated deep crouching and lateral collection can load knees, hips, adductors, lumbar spine, hands, and forearms for long periods.
sources: Wicket-Keeping in Cricket: A Literature Review
Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Wicket-Keeping

injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Catches, dives, boundary saves, and ball impact can cause finger, hand, shoulder, head, and lower-limb trauma. This is not solved only by strength; technique and exposure matter.
sources: Injuries in Cricket
Imaging in Elite and Recreational Cricket Injuries

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Youth early specialization and growth-spurt overload
injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Young cricketers need broad athletic development, not only more skill volume. Growth phases can temporarily reduce coordination and tissue tolerance.
sources: NSCA Position Statement on Long-Term Athletic Development
Injury Prevention Strategies for Adolescent Cricket Pace Bowlers

injury_or_load_risks.why_it_matters: Compressed schedules can combine travel, heat, sleep loss, repeated warm-ups, and limited tissue recovery. Plans should shift from development to maintenance and availability.
sources: Injuries in Cricket
Workout AI Backend Plan

training_implications.summary: Build general strength, trunk capacity, hip and shoulder mobility, aerobic base, sprint mechanics, hamstring and adductor strength, and broad athletic skills while cricket-specific load is lower.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: 2 to 4 gym sessions per week depending on level and role, with gradual running and throwing exposure maintained so re-entry is not abrupt.
sources: NSCA Injury Prevention Strategies in Cricket
NSCA Position Statement on Long-Term Athletic Development

training_implications.summary: Progressively reintroduce bowling, throwing, sprinting, catching, and match simulation. For fast bowlers, volume and intensity should build over weeks rather than jumping from gym-only work to match spells.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Progress balls, throws, sprint exposure, and match simulation one variable at a time where possible.
sources: Cricket Australia Junior Pace Bowling Workload Guidelines
ECB Recreational Fast Bowling Guidance 2024
Spikes in Acute Workload Are Associated With Increased Injury Risk in Elite Cricket Fast Bowlers

training_implications.summary: Maintain strength and power with lower total gym volume. Keep sprint and throwing exposure regular but not excessive. Adjust gym stress to match and practice load.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Use 1 to 3 strength exposures per week depending on match density, role, training age, and recovery.
sources: NSCA Injury Prevention Strategies in Cricket
Workout AI Backend Plan

training_implications.summary: The first 24 to 48 hours after heavy match exposure should emphasize rehydration, sleep, nutrition, soreness mapping, mobility, low-intensity movement, and symptom review before high-load training.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Do not add high-intensity conditioning or heavy lower-body strength if pain or readiness worsens after match day.
sources: Injuries in Cricket
Workout AI Backend Plan

training_implications.summary: Fast bowler gym work should include lower-body strength, unilateral strength, trunk stiffness, anti-rotation, controlled rotation, hip mobility, hamstring/calf capacity, shoulder/scapular work, and aerobic support.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Place heavy lower-body and trunk work away from the highest bowling intensity where possible.
sources: Physical Demands of Batting and Fast Bowling in Cricket
NSCA Injury Prevention Strategies in Cricket

training_implications.summary: Batters benefit from acceleration, sprint-turn mechanics, rotational power, trunk stiffness, med-ball throws, hamstring and calf capacity, and conditioning that preserves decision-making under repeated running.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Include short acceleration, braking, and turning exposures year-round at appropriate volume.
sources: Physical Demands of Batting and Fast Bowling in Cricket
Physical Profiling of International Cricket Players

training_implications.summary: Spinners need shoulder, trunk, hip, forearm, wrist, finger, and grip work, but the plan should avoid excessive local forearm fatigue before high-quality bowling sessions.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Use progressive forearm and wrist loading on non-heavy bowling days or after lower-priority skill work.
sources: Injuries in Cricket
NSCA Injury Prevention Strategies in Cricket

training_implications.summary: Wicketkeepers need hip and ankle mobility, adductor and quad endurance, trunk endurance, lateral power, hand/forearm capacity, and reaction work while managing deep-crouch fatigue.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Avoid stacking long keeping sessions with high-volume deep squats, heavy adductor work, and intense lateral plyometrics.
sources: Wicket-Keeping in Cricket: A Literature Review
Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Wicket-Keeping

training_implications.summary: Fielding preparation should include acceleration, braking, lateral movement, repeated sprint exposure, catching under movement, diving/landing progressions, and throwing progression.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Maintain small weekly doses in-season; build higher capacity in off-season and pre-season.
sources: Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Fielding

training_implications.summary: Shoulder programming should include scapular control, external and internal rotation strength, posterior shoulder capacity, thoracic mobility, trunk contribution, and progressive throwing.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Use low-fatigue shoulder work frequently; avoid heavy fatigue immediately before high-volume throwing or bowling.
sources: Shoulder Injuries in Modern Cricket
ASCA Review of Throwing Speed Determinants

training_implications.summary: Trunk training should balance anti-extension, anti-rotation, lateral endurance, controlled rotation, and power transfer. Fast bowlers and throwers need trunk capacity without excessive fatigue before skill exposure.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Rotate trunk emphases across the week; avoid maximal side-bending fatigue near bowling.
sources: Fast Bowling Kinematics and Lumbar Spine Injuries
Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Fielding

training_implications.summary: Useful tests include 10 m and 20 m sprint, repeated sprint ability, countermovement jump or broad jump, medicine-ball rotational throw, Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test, shoulder range and strength screen, trunk endurance, adductor squeeze, hamstring strength, throwing velocity, and role-specific bowling or batting load trend.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Use formal tests at block transitions and mini-monitoring weekly; compare against personal baseline and role demands.
sources: Physical Profiling of International Cricket Players
Anthropometry and Physical Profile of Elite Female Cricket Fast Bowlers
Strength and Conditioning for Cricket Fielding

training_implications.summary: Benchmarks should be tiered by level rather than absolute elite standards. A recreational player may need robust availability and stable sprint exposure more than elite Yo-Yo or jump scores.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Store percentile or level bands only when source population matches age, sex, role, and level; otherwise store result trend and coaching interpretation.
sources: Physical Profiling of International Cricket Players
Anthropometry and Physical Profile of Elite Female Cricket Fast Bowlers

training_implications.summary: After cricket practice or match play, athlete_state should update balls bowled, overs/spells, estimated throw count and intensity, batting running load, fielding sprint/dive exposure, session RPE, soreness map, pain changes, and readiness.
training_implications.preferred_dose_logic: Use the next workout to respond to the combined stress picture, not only prior gym completion.
sources: Workout AI Backend Plan
Is Bowling Workload a Risk Factor for Injury to Australian Junior Cricket Fast Bowlers
Relationship Between Cricket Workload and Injury Risk

backend_records_to_create.purpose: Store role-specific physical priorities, injury risks, skill-load conflicts, and match-week notes.
Create retrievable fast-bowling workload caps, build-up rules, and spike flags.
Track role-specific non-bowling skill loads that can affect injury risk and gym choices.
Map pain flags to plan adjustments, blocked training, and referral guidance.
Provide macro plan structure for off-season, pre-season, in-season, finals/tournament, transition, and return-to-play states.
Generate match-week microcycles that respect match timing and role-specific cricket exposure.
Provide staged return-to-bowling, return-to-throwing, and return-to-sprint templates with symptom gates.
Store cricket-relevant tests, measurement cadence, interpretation rules, and role-specific relevance.

open_questions.question: Which exact adult amateur bowling-load thresholds should be hard-coded versus retrieved from governing-body age and competition guidance?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Adult recreational cricket varies widely by format, league, pitch availability, and previous exposure.

open_questions.question: How should the backend handle acute:chronic workload ratio given ongoing debate in sports science?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The system should use workload trends and spikes pragmatically without presenting a single ratio as a diagnostic truth.

open_questions.question: What minimum data input is realistic for throw-count monitoring in a consumer app?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Manual throw counts may be burdensome, but ignoring throwing load misses a major cricket stressor.

open_questions.question: What role-specific normative benchmarks are available for youth, female, and recreational cricketers?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Most accessible performance profiling research is elite or small-sample, so personal baselines may be safer than broad cutoffs.

open_questions.question: Can spin-bowling workload be modeled better than simple ball count?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Variation type, gripping force, wet ball conditions, and wrist/finger symptoms may matter more than total deliveries alone.
